podcasts.title: Nick Bostrom: How Should We Navigate Superintelligence?
podcasts.description:
Nick Bostrom joins Theo Jaffee and Sofia Puccini on MTS to revisit the ideas about superintelligence and existential risk that he helped bring into the mainstream, now that increasingly capable AI systems actually exist.

Nick discusses why reinforcement learning may be pushing models toward more goal-seeking behavior, what recent agent experiments tell us about instrumental convergence, and why he favors preserving the ability to slow frontier development rather than committing now to a broad or indefinite AI pause. He also makes the case that the risks of AI need to be weighed alongside its potential upside, from advances in medicine and longer lifespans to entirely new ways of being human. 

They also get into whether today's models could already have some form of consciousness, the tradeoffs of open-source AI, whether machines can do original philosophy, mind uploading, and what the simulation hypothesis might mean for the superintelligence we create.

podcasts.description:
Is the future of frontier AI open or closed? ReflectionAI co-founder and CEO Misha Laskin joins Sarah Guo and Elad Gil to discuss the launch of Beam, the company’s 500 billion parameter open-weight reasoning model. Misha breaks down the pre-training and reinforcement learning required to produce Beam’s reasoning efficiency, the shift in enterprise compute from renting to owning intelligence, and how he believes that open models will capture the majority of global token demand. He also talks about the open model ecosystem in China and why competition with China’s models is a good thing, safety considerations around open models, and how frontier-level open models may accelerate the pace of scientific discovery.

podcasts.title: Chips, Memory, and Power | Pat Gelsinger
podcasts.description:
a16z's Raghu Raghuram and Guido Appenzeller sit down with Playground Global General Partner and former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger to discuss the next wave of semiconductor innovation and the physical constraints shaping the AI buildout.

Drawing on his experience designing Intel's 386 and 486 processors, Pat explains how AI could transform chip design, but also why faster design alone won't solve the industry's biggest problems. They examine the bottlenecks in manufacturing, memory bandwidth, advanced packaging, and power, and why today's explosion of specialized AI chips may eventually consolidate around a smaller number of architectures.

They also discuss the potential for new memory technologies, the shift from copper to optical networking, and why energy capacity could become a major constraint on AI growth. Finally, they revisit Pat's VMware years to ask what virtualization might look like when infrastructure is built for agents rather than humans.

podcasts.description:
Every day a new scientific breakthrough or existential threat seems to make the world more aware and more distrusting of an AI future that we’re told is rapidly approaching—whether we like it or not. And nobody is more recognized as the face of artificial intelligence—as a technology, an industry, and a civilizational shift—than Open AI founder and CEO Sam Altman. Long before he became a household name, Altman established a towering reputation in Silicon Valley: persuasive prodigy, visionary futurist, relentless CEO. But as OpenAI’s influence broke out of tech’s insular bubble, some of the very same traits that served him well in Northern California have become his greatest liabilities. In a far-ranging conversation taped in San Francisco on September 11th – the first of two sitdowns with Vanity Fair’s Mark Guiducci –  Altman discusses his views on ChatGPT and suicide prevention, safety breaches, and the film ‘Artificial,’ in which Andrew Garfield plays him—along with much more.  “I understand the instinct to say, ‘I don't want the change, I don't want the risk. Just stop it,’” Altman says. “I really hope that hundreds of years from now people look back at our lives and just can't believe how bad we had it.”

This is the first installment of a two-part interview with Altman. You can find the second installment on YouTube and podcast apps now.

✎ Jensen Huang was born in Taipei, Taiwan, before his family moved to Thailand. When he was nine years old, his parents sent him and his brother to live in America. They ended up at a reform school in Kentucky, where Jensen had to clean toilets every single day and deal with tough kids. After his parents moved to Oregon, Jensen worked as a dishwasher and waiter at Denny's for five years. He studied electrical engineering at Oregon State University and went to work designing computer chips. In 1993, Jensen met with two other engineers, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, at a Denny's to plan a new company. They raised money from Don Valentine at Sequoia Capital and started Nvidia with just $600.

✎ Nvidia faced major struggles right from the start. Their first graphics chip failed, and their second design was a bad fit for Sega video games. Jensen had to ask Sega's president, Shoichiro Irimajiri, to release them from their contract while still paying them $5 million. That money kept the business alive for six months, but Jensen still had to lay off more than half of his employees. The team put everything into building one last chip called the Riva 128, which saved Nvidia from shutting down. In 1999, the company went public and created the GeForce 256, which was the first graphics processing unit. They also built graphics hardware for the Microsoft Xbox.

✎ The decision to focus on artificial intelligence transformed Nvidia into a global tech leader. Jensen spent over $1 billion developing CUDA software so programmers could use graphics cards for heavy math problems.
